## Definition of ICI Rechallenge in HCC

ICI rechallenge is defined as **readministration of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy after either treatment failure or interruption of an initial ICI regimen** [P3]. It has emerged as a novel investigational approach in HCC immunotherapy for patients who discontinue initial immunotherapy due to disease progression, immune-related adverse events (irAEs), or treatment completion [P2][P3]. It is characterized as a rational and feasible therapeutic option for selected HCC patients, offering an opportunity for additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation [P1].

## Clinical Context and Rationale

ICI therapy is a cornerstone treatment for advanced HCC, acting by potentiating T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity against PD-1, PD-L1, and CTLA-4 pathways [P3]. However, many responders ultimately require discontinuation due to progressive disease (PD), irAEs, protocol-defined treatment completion, or other reasons, leaving limited therapeutic options [P3]. In this setting, rechallenge has been investigated as a salvage strategy [P3].

## Evidence Base and Outcomes

Existing clinical evidence comprises 10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, and 11 case reports, collectively encompassing 383 HCC patients with prior ICI exposure [P3]. Interruption causes of initial ICI treatment included PD in 64.5%, adverse events in 3.7%, other reasons in 2.3%, and unreported in 29.5% [P3]. Rechallenge achieved an ORR of 13.8%, DCR of 50.7%, mPFS of 2.0–5.6 months, and median OS of 7.4–16.7 months—generally lower than with initial ICI treatment, possibly due to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge [P3][F2]. However, several studies reported enhanced responses after rechallenge in individual patients, including CR/PR in patients who had PD as their best response to initial therapy [P3]. These pooled data should be interpreted cautiously, as no optimal indication or treatment strategy was applied across studies [P3].

## Treatment Strategies

Four main rechallenge strategies have been identified based on combinations of agents used initially and at rechallenge, most involving targeted therapy combined with anti-PD-L1 or dual ICIs [P2]. Proposed mechanisms include immunogenic cell death, tumor microenvironment remodeling, and re-expression of inhibitory checkpoints such as PD-L1 or CTLA-4 [P2]; mechanistically, regimens are categorized by combining targeted therapy with anti-PD-L1, switching between anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1, and dual CTLA-4/PD-(L)1 blockade [P8].

## Safety

During rechallenge, irAEs occurred in 54.1% and grade ≥3 irAEs in 19.5% of patients, higher than during initial ICI treatment (38.0% and 8.0%, respectively) [P4][F3]. The most common irAEs at rechallenge were skin irAEs (17.3%), enteritis (8.7%), and hepatitis (6.5%) [P4]. Despite this, only 1 (0.3%) fatal irAE was reported across studies, and most events were manageable with ICI discontinuation and corticosteroids [P4]. These findings may be influenced by selection bias and shorter follow-up [P4].

## Patient Selection

Favorable outcomes appear more frequent in patients with preserved liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI grades 1–2), age ≤60 years, and lower tumor burden [P2][P5]. An initial best response of PD is not a contraindication to rechallenge [P5], and prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication but warrant close monitoring [P5].

## Unresolved Questions

No standardized rechallenge regimen, patient indications, or fully elucidated mechanisms currently exist [P2][P3]. Many clinical and scientific questions remain unresolved despite demonstrated efficacy and acceptable safety in certain patients [P7]. Future research priorities include optimizing and expanding regimens (e.g., novel ICIs such as anti-TIGIT, anti-LAG3, bispecific antibodies, stroma modulators, and combination with local therapies), refining rechallenge timing, improving patient selection, and developing response biomarkers [P7].

## Number and Basis of ICI Rechallenge Strategies in HCC

**Four main strategies** are described for HCC, defined "according to the combinations of agents used in the initial and rechallenge treatments" [P1]. The same four-strategy framework is presented in the drug-selection analysis, where 378/383 (98.7%) patients received combination regimens and only 5 (1.3%) received single-agent rechallenge (durvalumab, pembrolizumab, or ipilimumab) [P2].

### The four strategies (by initial → rechallenge regimen) [P2]

| # | Initial treatment | Rechallenge regimen | n (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Anti-PD-1 immunotherapy | Targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 | 138 (36.0%) |
| 2 | Targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 | Anti-CTLA-4 ipilimumab + anti-PD-1 nivolumab | 100 (26.1%) |
| 3 | Bevacizumab + atezolizumab | Anti-CTLA-4 tremelimumab + anti-PD-L1 durvalumab | 132 (34.5%) |
| 4 | Targeted + anti-PD-L1 (same regimen) | Same regimen repeated after resistance | 13 (3.4%) |

Strategy 4 is described as "currently the only evidence of ICI rechallenge using the same regimen as the initial treatment" [P2]. Efficacy/safety figures for each regimen are reported in **Fig. 2c–e** (ORR, DCR, mPFS) and **Fig. 3c, d** (irAEs, grade ≥3 irAEs) [P2][F2]. Regimens 1 and 2 showed relatively higher ORR and a more favorable efficacy–safety balance, with grade ≥3 irAEs across all four regimens remaining within 15.0%–24.3% [P2].

### Important qualifications
- The classification is **descriptive of published studies**, not a validated framework: the review is based mainly on retrospective studies and case reports with substantial heterogeneity, and no statistical comparisons across regimens were performed [P2].
- No standardized rechallenge regimen or patient indications currently exist [P1][P3].
- **Not yet covered by any strategy:** there is currently no HCC rechallenge regimen combining ICI with interventional therapy, radiotherapy, or other local treatments; such combinations (e.g., sintilimab + stereotactic radiotherapy + IBI305 in an ongoing phase II trial) are proposed as future directions [P2][P4]. Proposed expansion also includes novel ICIs (anti-TIGIT, anti-LAG3, PD-(L)1/CTLA-4 bispecifics) and tumor-stroma modulators (TGF-β inhibitors, FAP-targeted agents, ECM-remodeling agents) [P4].

### Clinical framing and safety context
Rechallenge is characterized as "a rational and feasible therapeutic option for selected HCC patients" after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation, with future work needed on regimen selection and predictive biomarkers [P5][P1]. Regarding safety, irAE frequency is higher on rechallenge than on initial treatment (54.1% vs 38.0%; grade ≥3: 19.5% vs 8.0%), though fatal irAEs were fewer (1 case, 0.3%) [P6][F3]; most events were controllable with ICI discontinuation and corticosteroids, but these data may be affected by selection bias, shorter follow-up, and smaller cohorts [P6].

**Not stated in the evidence:** the specific biological rationale for choosing among the four strategies (mechanisms such as immunogenic cell death and TME remodeling are mentioned only generically [P1]), and any head-to-head comparative data across strategies [P2].

**Answer: Regimens 1 and 2 achieved relatively better outcomes among the four rechallenge strategies.**

**Direct comparison (the core finding)**
Among the four strategies, regimen 1 (targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1 following anti-PD-1 monotherapy) and regimen 2 (ipilimumab plus nivolumab after targeted and PD-L1 therapy) achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable clinical outcomes than regimen 3 (tremelimumab plus durvalumab after bevacizumab and atezolizumab) and regimen 4 (rechallenge with the same bevacizumab and atezolizumab regimen as initial treatment) [P1]. ICI rechallenge using combination strategies, particularly regimens 1 and 2, appeared to offer a more favorable balance between efficacy and safety [P1].

**Supporting outcome data by regimen** [P1]
- Regimen 1 (n = 138): ORR 17.4%, DCR 64.5%, mPF 5.2–5.6 months; irAEs 60.9%, grade ≥3 irAEs 18.8% [P1].
- Regimen 2 (n = 100): ORR 18.0%, DCR 45.0%, mPF 2.4–3.0 months; irAEs 44.8%, grade ≥3 irAEs 16.4% [P1].
- Regimen 3 (n = 132): ORR 6.8%, DCR 40.2%, mPF 2.0–4.0 months; irAEs 51.4%, grade ≥3 irAEs 24.3% [P1].
- Regimen 4 (n = 13): ORR 15.0%, DCR 54.0%, mPF 4.7 months; irAEs 46.0%, grade ≥3 irAEs 15.0% [P1].

Severe (grade ≥3) irAEs remained within 15.0%–24.3% across all four regimens, indicating an overall manageable safety profile [P1].

**Important caveats on interpretation**
The review is mainly based on retrospective studies and case reports, with substantial heterogeneity and no statistical comparisons performed across regimens; findings should therefore be interpreted with caution [P1]. The four-strategy framework itself derives from combinations of agents used in initial versus rechallenge treatment, most involving targeted therapy plus anti-PD-L1 or dual ICIs [P2]. Clinical benefit appears more frequent in patients with preserved liver function, age <60 years, and lower tumor burden, again requiring cautious interpretation due to interstudy heterogeneity and selection bias [P2]; consistent with this, good liver function (Child-Pugh A, ALBI grades 1–2), younger age (≤60 years), and lower tumor burden were associated with more favorable outcomes, and good liver function was the most consistent prognostic predictor across studies [P8]. Prior irAEs were not an absolute contraindication to rechallenge but warrant close monitoring [P8].

**Scope and limitations of the evidence base**
No ICI rechallenge regimen in HCC currently combines ICI with interventional therapy, radiotherapy, or other local treatments [P1]; future expansion should focus on rationally designed combinations integrating immune modulation, targeted inhibition, and TME remodeling (e.g., novel ICIs such as anti-TIGIT, anti-LAG3, or PD-(L)1/CTLA-4 bispecifics, and stroma-modulating agents) [P6]. Future research should focus on optimizing regimen selection, refining predictive biomarkers, and elucidating the molecular basis of immune reactivation [P7].

**Note on the remaining cited items**
The retrieved evidence does not contain data bearing on the query from several of the items flagged for citation, and they are therefore noted rather than analyzed as substantive support: [P3] reports a systematic review of non-clinical self-management strategies for menstrual cycle symptoms (unrelated population and interventions); [P4] concerns prognosis in primary CNS lymphoma; [P5] concerns vancomycin pharmacokinetic dosing simulations in neonates; [P9] concerns rechallenge after immune checkpoint inhibitor pneumonitis (recommended only after complete resolution of grade 2 ICI-P) [P9]. No figure or table evidence ([F2]) relevant to the four HCC rechallenge regimens was retrieved; the regimen-level outcome data above are drawn from the text and its cited supplementary tables [P1].

**Pooled (review-level) comparison**

In the pooled analysis across the reviewed HCC studies, the ORR of initial ICI treatment was 20.3% [P1], whereas ICI rechallenge achieved an ORR of 13.8% [P1]. The review states that patients receiving rechallenge had lower ORR, lower DCR, and shorter mPFS than those receiving initial ICI treatment, attributing this to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge [P1]. These pooled figures are derived from multiple heterogeneous studies, and the authors caution that no optimal indication or treatment strategy was applied across them [P1]. The review's summary further notes that rechallenge has shown "variable but notable antitumor activity" across published studies, with benefit more frequent in patients with preserved liver function, age <60 years, and lower tumor burden, while cautioning about interstudy heterogeneity and selection bias [P4].

**Study-level comparisons (rechallenge vs. initial ICI)**

- Scheiner et al. [28]: superior ORR with rechallenge vs. initial ICI therapy (26% vs. 22%), including 11 PR cases among 21 patients who had progressed on initial ICI [P1].
- Alden et al. [32]: markedly higher ORR with rechallenge (22%) vs. initial ICI therapy (6%), with 4 of 18 PD patients achieving objective response [P1].
- Wong et al. [31]: BOR to initial ICI was PD, yet CR or PR to rechallenge was observed in a subset of patients (no ORR percentage stated) [P1].
- Roessler et al. [33] and Suzuki et al. [39]: individual patients with SD or PD on initial ICI subsequently achieved CR/PR on rechallenge (no comparative ORR stated) [P1].

**Regimen-specific rechallenge ORRs (no paired initial-therapy ORR reported)**

- Regimen 1 (targeted + anti-PD-L1 after anti-PD-1 monotherapy): ORR 17.4% [P3].
- Regimen 2 (ipilimumab + nivolumab after targeted/PD-L1 therapy): ORR 18.0% [P3].
- Regimen 3 (tremelimumab + durvalumab after bevacizumab/atezolizumab): ORR 6.8% [P3].
- Regimen 4 (same bevacizumab + atezolizumab regimen): ORR 15.0% [P3].
Among the four strategies, regimens 1 and 2 achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable outcomes than regimens 3 and 4 [P3].

**Rechallenge-interval subgroup ORRs**

With an interval <1 month, rechallenge ORR was 20.0%; with an interval >1 month, ORR was 19.1% [P2].

**Interpretation and limitations**

The review concludes that ICI rechallenge is a rational and feasible option for selected HCC patients, offering additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation [P5], while emphasizing that the evidence is mainly retrospective with substantial heterogeneity and no statistical comparisons across regimens, so findings should be interpreted cautiously [P3]. Notably, the direction of the comparison is inconsistent across sources: pooled data favor initial therapy (20.3% vs. 13.8%) [P1], whereas individual studies (Scheiner, Alden) report higher ORR with rechallenge [P1]; the review does not state a pooled statistical test reconciling these, and the discrepant estimates derive from different study populations and regimens [P1][P3]. Figure 2 (panels a, c) is cited in the text as the source for the initial-treatment and rechallenge ORR data [P1][P3], but the figure's numerical content is not reproduced in the retrieved evidence, so panel-level values cannot be verified here.

# Why Patient Selection Matters for ICI Rechallenge in HCC

## 1. Core rationale: outcomes are driven by baseline characteristics and tumor biology
Optimal selection of HCC patients is described as "critical for maximizing the efficacy of ICI rechallenge, as clinical outcomes are profoundly influenced by baseline patient characteristics and tumor biology" [P3][S1]. Improving patient selection is also listed among the unresolved priorities for future research, alongside regimen optimization, rechallenge timing, and response biomarkers [P1].

## 2. Selection factors supported in HCC
- **Liver function (most consistent predictor):** Child-Pugh A and lower ALBI grades were associated with longer OS after rechallenge in two regimens [P3].
- **Age and tumor burden:** Age ≤60 years and intrahepatic tumor number ≤10 were independent protective factors for OS [P3].
- **Inflammation:** NLR <3.1 was an independent protective factor for OS [P3].
- **Reason for initial discontinuation:** In HCC, nearly half of patients who stopped initial ICI for PD had BOR of PD at rechallenge, whereas all 5 who stopped for adverse events achieved disease control—though the small sample size limits reliability [P2]. Progression pattern (existing lesions, new lesions, vascular invasion) may also influence benefit [P2].
- **Prior response remains controversial:** An initial BOR of PD is not a contraindication, since some patients with initial PD still responded to rechallenge [P3].
- **Safety-based selection:** Prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication but warrant close monitoring and individualized risk–benefit assessment [P3].

## 3. Required additional evidence (explicitly addressed)

**Selection bias in the rechallenge evidence base [P5]:** Rechallenge decisions remain "highly individualized and controversial," and the evidence is "primarily derived from retrospective cohorts, with significant selection bias and confounding by indication"; recurrence rates vary widely (30–50%) and no validated risk-stratification tool exists [P5]. This is precisely why rigorous patient selection—rather than extrapolation from biased cohorts—is needed.

**Biomarker-based rather than diagnosis-based selection [P8]:** Because the TME varies by genotype, treatment history, and resistance state, "patient selection should be based on prespecified biomarkers rather than on a generic diagnosis," using composite measures (e.g., PD-L1, TAM infiltration, hypoxia/lactate signatures) treated as exploratory hypotheses until prospectively validated [P8]. This parallels the HCC review's call for developing response biomarkers [P1].

**Analogy from other disease contexts [P7]:** In neutrophilic asthma, "current and emerging biologics require careful patient selection based on inflammatory phenotype," with agents reserved for specific endotypes and some requiring biomarker-guided selection [P7]—illustrating the general principle that phenotype-matched selection determines whether a therapy is appropriate.

**Individualized titration/selection for tolerability [P6]:** For incretin-based therapies, favourable safety is maintained "through individualized dose titration and careful patient selection" [P6]—supporting the broader principle that selection and individualized management reduce avoidable toxicity, analogous to the irAE-based selection considerations in HCC rechallenge [P3].

**Mechanistic rationale for selection by resistance mechanism [P9]:** ICD magnitude is positively associated with anti-PD-1 responsiveness in preclinical melanoma models, and tumors with JAK1/JAK2 deficiency or STING silencing show differential sensitivity to oncolytic virotherapy [P9]. This supports selecting patients according to the dominant resistance mechanism, since benefit depends on which resistance pathway is operative.

**Note on figure [F2]:** No figure or table with the identifier F2 appears in the retrieved evidence; therefore no figure-level data can be cited. The only figure present is Figure 1 in [P9], which depicts ICD mechanisms and immune-cell recruitment rather than patient-selection data.

## 4. What the evidence does not cover
The retrieved evidence does not establish validated selection criteria or cut-offs for ICI rechallenge in HCC; PD-L1, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, microsatellite stability, and mutational load are noted as predictors of *initial* ICI benefit but with "little known" about their role in rechallenge [P3]. Prospective, multicenter, large-scale trials are required to optimize selection [P2][P3].

# Role of Liquid Biopsy with ctDNA in Advanced HCC

## 1. Rationale: compensating for the absence of routine tissue profiling
Tumor tissue biopsy is not mandatory for HCC diagnosis, which makes genomic precision medicine in advanced HCC more challenging [P2][P3]. Liquid biopsy — molecular profiling of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) shed from tumors into the circulation — may provide a noninvasive, safe alternative for cancer genomic profiling and thus compensate for the lack of routine tissue-based genomic profiling in HCC [P2]. The liver's abundant blood supply and tumor-related hepatocyte necrosis drive abundant tumor-derived cfDNA into peripheral blood, making HCC particularly suitable for cfDNA-based detection [P1].

## 2. Concordance with tumor tissue (the central evidence gap)
Few investigations have assessed concordance between next-generation sequencing (NGS) results from liquid biopsy and tumor tissue in HCC; existing studies are constrained by limited sample numbers and restricted target gene sets, hampering comparison of ctDNA versus tissue NGS [P2]. One prospective cohort (130 patients with advanced HCC, pretreatment plasma, tissue-based sequencing before systemic therapy, June 2020–October 2022) was designed specifically to evaluate ctDNA–tissue concordance and feasibility in patients treated with atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (atezo/bev) [P3]. **Note:** the retrieved evidence provides only the introduction/methods of this study; its concordance and prognostic results are not stated.

## 3. Clinical positioning: prognostic/investigational, not yet actionable
Liquid biopsy, particularly ctDNA, offers a minimally invasive approach for assessing tumor-derived molecular signals and potential minimal residual disease (MRD) [P7]. Postoperative ctDNA positivity is associated with increased recurrence risk after curative-intent treatment, but reported sensitivity varies substantially across studies due to differences in assay design, tumor shedding, and analytical methods [P7]. Accordingly, ctDNA is currently a promising **investigational** biomarker for recurrence-risk stratification and MRD assessment, rather than a validated basis for altering surgery or adjuvant treatment in routine HCC practice [P7]. More broadly, such biological approaches remain primarily prognostic, investigational, or hypothesis-generating, and integration into treatment decisions requires prospective validation that biomarker-guided interventions improve clinically meaningful outcomes [P7][S2].

## 4. Analytical modalities and heterogeneity
Three mainstream cfDNA detection modalities exist — mutation analysis, tissue-specific methylation profiling, and fragmentomics — each capturing distinct tumor-specific molecular features [P1]. Although cfDNA's diagnostic value for HCC is supported, marked interstudy heterogeneity persists, and direct comparisons of the three strategies (particularly in early HCC) remain unclear [P1]. This heterogeneity is a key caveat when extrapolating performance to the advanced setting.

## 5. Required additional evidence items

**P4 (breast cancer miRNA study):** This passage addresses liquid biopsy in breast cancer, not HCC. It states that liquid biopsy-based biomarkers offer a minimally invasive alternative capable of capturing dynamic tumor biology [P4], but its analyte is circulating microRNAs, not ctDNA, and its population is breast cancer. It therefore provides **no direct evidence on ctDNA in advanced HCC** and is cited here only to delimit scope: general claims about "liquid biopsy" in other tumor types should not be transferred to HCC ctDNA without HCC-specific data.

**P5 (ctRNA in HCC/CCA):** This study positions circulating cell-free tumor **RNA** as a novel and emerging alternative to circulating cell-free tumor DNA for detecting the presence and understanding the biology of liver tumors [P5]. It identified a short circulating mutated RNA panel able to distinguish liver cancer patients in a discovery cohort and validated splicing aberrations (including intron retentions) in tumor tissue; the authors state the plasma assays, if confirmed in larger cohorts, could be used to identify patients with HCC [P5]. Relevance to advanced HCC ctDNA: it indicates that ctDNA is not the only circulating nucleic-acid analyte under development, and that RNA-based approaches may capture splicing-level changes not transcribed from DNA [P5]. However, this evidence concerns detection/identification rather than advanced-stage treatment selection, and confirmation in larger cohorts is explicitly pending [P5].

**P10 (HCC exosomes):** HCC cells release oncogenic exosomes that establish tumor–stroma crosstalk and remodel the tumor microenvironment, promoting proliferation, angiogenesis, and metastatic dissemination; this vesicle-mediated communication also creates opportunities for liquid-biopsy biomarkers and engineered therapeutic nanocarriers [P10]. Relevance: extracellular vesicles represent a parallel, non-ctDNA liquid-biopsy compartment in HCC, and exosome biology is shaped by heterogeneity in cellular origin, cargo, surface markers, and disease-stage-dependent release [P10]. This heterogeneity argument is analogous to the assay/shedding variability that limits ctDNA sensitivity [P7], but P10 provides no ctDNA-specific performance data in advanced HCC.

**F2 (figure):** No figure content was retrieved in the supplied evidence. **Not stated** — the figure's data cannot be summarized or cited substantively; only its existence is referenced in the source list.

## 6. Summary
In advanced HCC, ctDNA-based liquid biopsy is best supported as (i) a noninvasive route to genomic profiling that could substitute for non-mandatory tissue biopsy [P2][P3], and (ii) an investigational prognostic/MRD tool [P7]. Its clinical validity as a treatment-selection instrument in advanced HCC is **not established** in the retrieved evidence; concordance data from the dedicated atezo/bev cohort are not reported here [P3], and alternative analytes (ctRNA, exosomes) remain exploratory [P5][P10].

# Limits on Precision Medicine in HCC per the ctDNA Paper

## 1. Core structural barrier: no mandatory tissue biopsy
The ctDNA study frames the central obstacle as diagnostic practice rather than technology: precision medicine in HCC is "hindered by the lack of mandatory tissue biopsy for genomic profiling in HCC" [P4]. Because tumor tissue biopsy is not required for HCC diagnosis, genomic profiling is not routinely obtained, "making precision medicine more challenging" [P3]. The authors position liquid biopsy as a compensatory, noninvasive alternative for this gap [P3][P4].

## 2. Limited concordance between ctDNA and tissue
Concordance was clinically acceptable but imperfect: 72.6% sensitivity and 75.0% PPV excluding TERT promoter mutations, falling to 64.3% sensitivity and 67.9% PPV when TERT promoter mutations were included [P6]. Discordance was attributed to:
- **TERT promoter sequencing difficulty** — high GC content complicates detection in ctDNA [P6].
- **Sampling interval** — restricting to ≤30 days raised sensitivity to 96.3% [P6].
- **Tissue specimen type** — biopsy specimens showed high sensitivity/low PPV; surgical specimens low sensitivity/high PPV (PPV 85.4–100% vs. 66.7–70.6%) [P6].
- **CNVs** — low concordance, reflecting low CNV frequency and inherent technical/biological limits of ctDNA for CNVs and gene fusions [P6].

## 3. No druggable targets → limited therapeutic utility
"Because HCC lacks established druggable targets, the therapeutic utility of ctDNA remains limited," and prognostic biomarkers such as maxVAF require validation in larger independent cohorts as predictive tools [P6]. MaxVAF's prognostic utility is supported, but its *predictive* value is not established [P6].

## 4. Assay and platform constraints
Only Guardant360 CDx and FoundationOne Liquid CDx are FDA-approved; HCC "often includes low ctDNA fractions and infrequent actionable alterations" [P6]. Tissue-informed MRD assays (e.g., Signatera) "may have limited applicability in advanced HCC, which is often diagnosed without biopsy-confirmed tissue samples" [P6].

## 5. Study-level limitations
East Asian, HBV-endemic cohort only, requiring external validation; single pretreatment blood sample precluding inference on causes of discordance; possible residual CHIP effects; limited statistical power in subgroup analyses [P6].

## 6. Corroborating evidence from other retrieved papers
- **General biomarker gap in immunotherapy**: "The absence of reliable biomarkers to anticipate primary resistance, detect emerging secondary resistance, or guide rational sequencing and combination strategies further limits the precision of immunotherapy" [P2]. Validated predictive tools for benefit and irAE risk are lacking [P2].
- **ctDNA remains investigational in HCC**: ctDNA is "a promising investigational biomarker for recurrence-risk stratification and MRD assessment, rather than a validated basis for altering surgery or adjuvant treatment in routine HCC practice"; reported sensitivity varies with assay design, tumor shedding, and analytical methods [P7].
- **Tumor heterogeneity**: HCC is "a highly heterogeneous tumor with high cellular diversity, a key factor in therapeutic failures"; TFEB-driven plasticity/heterogeneity underlies poor outcomes, and identifying this subset for TFEB/TFE3 inhibition is proposed as a precision-medicine route [P8].
- **Exosome-based approaches**: exosomal heterogeneity (cellular origin, cargo, tropism, disease stage) determines divergent effects, and external validation plus standardized analytical pipelines are needed before clinical translation of exosomal miRNA biomarkers [P5].

## 7. Items not covered by the retrieved evidence
The following routed items contain no HCC- or ctDNA-specific content and therefore cannot be used to answer this question:
- **[P1]** — feline oral microbiome diagnostics; its caveats (selection bias in convenience samples, non-standardized phenotyping, single-time-point sampling) concern veterinary oral disease, not HCC.
- **[P9]** — neutrophilic asthma microbiome interventions; the statement that "the non-specific nature of antibiotics limits long-term utility" concerns airway infection, not HCC.
- **[F2]** — no figure/table with this ID appears in the retrieved evidence; no data can be cited from it.

**Summary**: According to the ctDNA paper, precision medicine in HCC is limited chiefly by the absence of routine tissue-based genomic profiling, imperfect and context-dependent ctDNA–tissue concordance (TERT promoter, sampling interval, specimen type, CNVs), the lack of druggable targets restricting ctDNA's therapeutic utility, assay/platform constraints in low-shedding disease, and unvalidated predictive biomarkers — with the broader immunotherapy literature independently identifying biomarker gaps and tumor heterogeneity as parallel barriers [P2][P5][P6][P7][P8].

# EV Cargo and Its Importance in Breast Cancer

## 1. What cargo do EVs carry?

**General cargo classes.** EVs are lipid-bilayered, membrane-bound particles secreted by diverse cell types that carry **proteins, lipids, DNA, and RNA**, and they mediate intercellular communication by transporting bioactive cargo between cells [P2]. This is echoed in the breast cancer (BC) context: EVs "carry biologically active cargo such as RNAs and proteins" [P5], and their payload is described as a "multimolecular payload reflecting cellular status and intercellular communication" [P9]. More granularly, exosomes (an EV subset) incorporate nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids [P3], and deliver "miRNAs, mRNAs, proteins, and lipids" to recipient cells [P7].

**RNA cargo.** In BC specifically, the RNA cargo includes:
- **miRNAs** — small non-coding RNAs (~18–24 nt) that bind target mRNAs to suppress translation [P10];
- **lncRNAs** — >200 nt non-coding RNAs that regulate gene expression by "sponging" miRNAs (ceRNA mechanism) [P10];
- **circRNAs** — covalently closed loop RNAs lacking 5′ caps/3′ poly(A) tails, highly resistant to exonuclease degradation and often enriched in EVs including exosomes and microvesicles [P10].

EVs **protect their RNA cargo from degradation** in the extracellular environment and transfer RNAs between cells [P10].

**Protein cargo.** Proteomic analysis of small EV (sEV) proteins from BC cell lines identified metastasis-associated proteins including **Ezrin, annexin A5, annexin A6, tenascin, and EMMPRIN/CD147** [P10]. Large EVs (lEVs) transport **surface antigens, oncogenic products, and adhesion molecules** on their surface or within vesicles [P2]. Immune-related protein cargo includes **PD-L1** on tumor exosomes [P1] and EV-associated immune checkpoints such as **PD-1 and CD80** on immunocyte-derived sEVs [P8].

**Subpopulation framing.** In BC, distinct EV subpopulations — mainly sEVs (~50–200 nm), lEVs (~150–500 nm), and apoptotic bodies (~500–4000 nm) — play distinct roles in tumour progression and metastasis [P2]. The review explicitly uses sEV/lEV as size-based categories per MISEV guidelines rather than definitive origin indicators, and notes that isolation methods may also recover non-vesicular particles such as exomeres and supermeres [P2].

## 2. Why is this cargo important in breast cancer?

**Intercellular communication and phenotypic reprogramming.** EVs reflect the molecular composition of their cell of origin and act as messengers contributing to cancer progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis [P2]. lEVs and sEVs deliver bioactive cargo associated with progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis [P2]. Cargo molecules are internalised by recipient cells, where they **modify the recipient cell phenotype and modulate the metastatic cascade** [P10]. Collectively, EV RNAs constitute a coordinated network transferred to recipient cells to reprogramme post-transcriptional gene expression and facilitate pro-metastatic signalling [P10].

**Specific metastatic functions.**
- sEVs in distant target organs facilitate **integrin uptake**, establishing the microenvironment required for initial metastasis via seeding tumour cells [P2].
- lEVs deliver surface antigens, oncogenic products, and adhesion molecules to distant sites, playing a crucial role in invasion and metastasis [P2].
- EVs contribute to the tumour microenvironment, **premetastatic niche formation, immune evasion, extracellular matrix remodelling**, and ultimately promote BC organotropism [P5].
- Fig. 1 (as described in text) summarizes that BC-derived sEVs and lEVs deliver RNAs and proteins to neighbouring cells, remodelling the TME by inducing immune suppression, migration and invasion, and promoting pre-metastatic niche formation; miRNAs and proteins in EVs are also associated with organotropic niche conditioning and distant colonisation [P10].

**Immune modulation (dualistic).** Tumor-derived EVs carry immunosuppressive cargo facilitating immune evasion — e.g., tumor exosomes displaying PD-L1 inhibit cytotoxic T cells — while exosomes bearing MHC class I-restricted tumor antigens can activate T cells and provoke antitumor responses; thus tumor-derived EVs may act either as agents of immune escape or triggers of antitumor immunity, context-dependently [P1]. In BC specifically, Munc13-4 was identified as a trafficking regulator promoting PD-L1 sorting and secretion via exosomes; its genetic deletion in breast cancer enhanced T cell–mediated antitumor immunity, suppressed tumor growth, and improved immune checkpoint inhibitor efficacy [P8]. PD-L1⁺ tumor-derived EVs can also mediate resistance to anti–PD-L1 therapy by acting as antibody "decoys" [P8]. PD-1/CD80⁺ sEVs induce downregulation of adhesion and antigen-presentation molecules on tumor cells and impaired immune infiltration, converting tumors to an immunologically cold phenotype [P8].

**Clinical relevance.** Growing evidence highlights EVs as potential **diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers and viable therapeutic targets** in BC [P5]; EV biomarkers can capture cell-of-origin signals while encoding systemic communication programs [P9]. # Main Global Challenges in CRC Burden Despite Screening

## 1. Persistent absolute burden despite screening gains
CRC remains one of the most common malignancies (~10% of all cancer cases) and the second leading cause of cancer-related death globally, with >1.9 million new cases and >900,000 deaths estimated in 2022 [P1][P2][P4]. Screening has reduced incidence and mortality in older adults, yet the absolute global burden remains high [P2][P5].

## 2. Demographic aging, unequal access, and modifiable risk exposure
The high residual burden is attributed to demographic aging, unequal access to care, and persistent exposure to modifiable risks [P5]. Screening coverage varies widely: high uptake in some high-income countries versus persistently low participation in many low- and middle-income settings, with within-country socioeconomic and demographic disparities exacerbating inequalities [P6].

## 3. Early-onset CRC
Early-onset CRC has emerged as a major challenge, with the relative contribution and causal importance of life-course environmental, metabolic, inflammatory, and microbial exposures remaining incompletely defined [P5][P2].

## 4. A paradoxical epidemiological pattern
CRC epidemiology shows declining rates in screened populations alongside an increasing global burden, particularly among younger individuals and in transitioning economies—reflecting demographic change, lifestyle transitions, and unequal healthcare access [P10].

## 5. Screening test limitations
Blood-based screening (cfDNA Shield assay) showed 83.1% sensitivity for CRC but only 13.2% sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions, with 89.6% specificity; it is positioned as participation-enhancing rather than equivalent to FIT/colonoscopy, and long-term effects on interval cancer and mortality remain under evaluation [P9].

## 6. Treatment-refractory disease and clinical gaps
Metastatic CRC remains associated with poor long-term outcomes, particularly in patients not benefiting from ICIs [P1]. Additional challenges include low early diagnosis rates, drug resistance, and the limited proportion of immunotherapy responders [P4]. MSS/pMMR tumors (the majority) remain largely refractory to ICI monotherapy, with response rates generally below 10% [P8].

## 7. Biological and host factors sustaining burden
Epidemiological patterns are closely linked to metabolic dysfunction, inflammation, and microbiota alterations [P10]. Consistent with this, CRC patients show a systemic inflammatory/immunosuppressive phenotype, with altered short-chain fatty acid profiles (e.g., reduced propionate inversely correlated with IL-6/IL-13) [P7].

The retrieved evidence does not quantify screening-attributable mortality reductions by region, nor does it provide cost-effectiveness data. [P3] concerns hepatocellular carcinoma, not CRC, and therefore does not contribute CRC-specific burden evidence; no figure [F2] was present in the retrieved evidence, so figure-level data could not be cited.

# Efficacy vs. Safety Evidence for ICI Rechallenge in HCC

## 1. Efficacy evidence

**Pooled activity is modest and inferior to initial ICI therapy.** Across 10 retrospective studies, 2 prospective studies, and 11 case reports (383 patients), rechallenge achieved ORR 13.8%, DCR 50.7%, mPFS 2.0–5.6 months, and mOS 7.4–16.7 months, versus ORR 20.3%, DCR 69.0%, and mPFS 3.7–5.4 months with initial ICI treatment [P8]. The review attributes this to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge [P8], and cautions that these are pooled data without a uniform indication or strategy [P8].

**Regimen-dependent efficacy.** In the 12 clinical studies, 378/383 (98.7%) patients received combination regimens [P3]. ORR/DCR/mPFS were 17.4%/64.5%/5.2–5.6 months (Regimen 1), 18.0%/45.0%/2.4–3.0 months (Regimen 2), 6.8%/40.2%/2.0–4.0 months (Regimen 3), and 15.0%/54.0%/4.7 months (Regimen 4) [P3]. Regimens 1 and 2 gave the more favorable efficacy–safety balance, but the authors note substantial heterogeneity and no statistical cross-regimen comparison [P3].

**Interval effect.** Intervals >1 month were associated with longer mPFS (3.7–5.4 vs. 2.9–3.0 months) and higher DCR (62.5% vs. 40.0%), with similar ORR (19.1% vs. 20.0%) [P4].

**Selected-patient signals.** Individual studies reported rechallenge ORR exceeding initial ORR (26% vs. 22%; 22% vs. 6%), including responses in patients who had progressed initially [P8]. Efficacy may differ by reason for discontinuation: of 11 patients stopping initial ICI for PD, nearly half had BOR of PD at rechallenge, whereas all 5 stopping for adverse events achieved SD — a speculative inference limited by small sample size [P6]. Favorable outcomes are associated with preserved liver function, age ≤60 years, and lower tumor burden [P9].

**Comparative efficacy vs. TKIs is unproven.** No head-to-head study exists in HCC; an international retrospective study reported mPPS 14.9 vs. 8.4 months (rechallenge vs. TKI) but the difference was not significant (p = 0.25), and the phase III CONTACT-03 trial in renal cell carcinoma found rechallenge was not better than TKI [P1].

## 2. Safety evidence

**irAE frequency increases with rechallenge, but severity is bounded.** irAEs/grade ≥3 irAEs were 38.0%/8.0% during initial ICI treatment versus 54.1%/19.5% at rechallenge [P5]. By regimen, irAE and grade ≥3 irAE rates were 60.9%/18.8% (Regimen 1), 44.8%/16.4% (Regimen 2), 51.4%/24.3% (Regimen 3), and 46.0%/15.0% (Regimen 4); severe irAEs remained within 15.0–24.3% across all four regimens, described as an overall manageable profile [P3].

**Fatal irAEs were rarer than with initial treatment.** Only 1 (0.3%) fatal irAE occurred across the 12 studies and 11 case reports, versus 3.1% after initial ICI treatment; most rechallenge irAEs were controllable with ICI interruption and corticosteroids [P5]. The irAE spectrum was comparable to initial treatment (most common: skin 17.3%, enteritis 8.7%, hepatitis 6.5%) [P5].

**Safety is not interval-dependent.** The safety profile did not differ significantly between <1-month and >1-month interval groups (grade ≥3 irAEs 11.4% vs. 14.7%) [P4].

**Prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication.** Of 7 patients (22%) with prior irAEs, 3 developed recurrent irAEs on ipilimumab–nivolumab rechallenge, mostly corticosteroid-manageable without stopping treatment [P9].

**Key caveat — selection bias.** Patients with severe irAEs tended not to be readministered, so the rechallenge population may be enriched for tolerability; results may also be affected by shorter follow-up and smaller cohorts [P5].

## 3. Direct comparison of the two evidence streams

| Dimension | Efficacy | Safety |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of change vs. initial ICI | Inferior (ORR 13.8% vs. 20.3%; shorter mPFS) [P8] | Worse frequency (irAEs 54.1% vs. 38.0%; G≥3 19.5% vs. 8.0%) [P5] but fewer fatal events (0.3% vs. 3.1%) [P5] |
| Consistency across regimens | Variable (ORR 6.8–18.0%) [P3] | Relatively uniform severity (G≥3 15.0–24.3%) [P3] |
| Modifiability | Improved with interval >1 month [P4]; patient selection (liver function, age, tumor burden) [P9] | Not significantly modified by interval [P4]; manageable with monitoring/steroids [P5] |
| Strength of evidence | Retrospective/real-world dominated; no RCT; no head-to-head vs. TKI [P1][P3] | Same limitation; confounded by selection bias and short follow-up [P5] |

**Overall verdict in the source.** The review concludes that ICI rechallenge has shown both efficacy and acceptable safety in certain HCC patients, while many questions remain unresolved [P2]; it characterizes the strategy as having "variable but notable antitumor activity with an acceptable safety profile," with increased irAE frequency but mostly manageable events [P7]. Thus the safety evidence is comparatively more consistent (bounded severe-toxicity rates, low fatality, predictable management) than the efficacy evidence, which is heterogeneous, generally inferior to initial ICI therapy, and supported mainly by retrospective data without randomized or TKI-controlled confirmation [P1][P3][P8].

## 4. Not covered by the evidence
- No RCT or prospective head-to-head trial of rechallenge versus TKI in HCC [P1].
- No validated biomarker for either rechallenge benefit or toxicity in HCC; lymphatic/tertiary lymphoid structure and ctDNA predictors remain unestablished in HCC, and autoantibody/HLA toxicity predictors derive from melanoma and RCC cohorts [P1].
- No data on rechallenge combined with local therapies in HCC (only an ongoing phase II trial) [P3].

**Short answer: No — benefit is not universal.** ICI rechallenge is described as a rational and feasible option only for *selected* HCC patients, and the evidence base is explicitly limited by heterogeneity, selection bias, and the absence of standardized indications or randomized data.

**1. Benefit is restricted to selected patients, not all**
- Rechallenge is characterized as "a rational and feasible therapeutic option for **selected** HCC patients, providing an opportunity to achieve additional clinical benefit after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation" [P1][S1].
- Across published studies, rechallenge showed "**variable** but notable antitumor activity with an acceptable safety profile" [P2] — i.e., variable, not uniform, activity.
- The review states that "ICI rechallenge has shown both efficacy and acceptable safety in **certain** HCC patients," and that "many clinical and scientific questions remain unresolved" [P4].

**2. Factors associated with more favorable outcomes (candidate selection criteria)**
- Good liver function (Child-Pugh A; ALBI grades 1–2), younger age (≤60 years), and lower tumor burden may be associated with better outcomes; Child-Pugh A and lower ALBI grade were associated with longer OS, and age ≤60 years plus intrahepatic tumor number ≤10 were independent protective factors for OS [P5].
- NLR <3.1 was an independent protective factor for OS in one study [P5].
- "Across studies, good liver function has been the most consistent prognostic predictor" [P5].
- Prior irAEs are "not an absolute contraindication" but warrant close monitoring and individualized risk–benefit assessment [P5].

**3. What limits the conclusion**
- **No standardized regimen or patient indications**, and few mechanistic studies [P2].
- **Interstudy heterogeneity and potential selection bias**: the favorable-profile findings "require cautious interpretation due to interstudy heterogeneity and potential selection bias" [P2].
- **Controversial/conflicting predictor — initial BOR:** Lai et al. reported prior response to initial anti-PD-1 as an independent protective factor for OS (but not PFS), and Ho et al. found initial PD patients all had PD at rechallenge while initial SD patients achieved 60% DCR [P5]; in contrast, Wong et al. found neither primary nor acquired resistance associated with OS [P5]. The review concludes only that "an initial BOR of PD is not a contraindication" [P5]. A short duration of disease control initially "did not necessarily preclude" benefit [P5].
- **Reason for discontinuation may matter, but evidence is weak:** Miura et al. found nearly half of PD-discontinuation patients had PD at rechallenge, whereas all 5 AE-discontinuation patients achieved SD — but "the small sample size in that study limited the reliability of these findings" [P6]. Progression patterns (existing lesions, new lesions, vascular invasion) may also influence benefit [P6].
- **Timing unresolved:** no definitive conclusion on when to start rechallenge; intervals ranged 0.7–20.1 months, and no study reports direct rechallenge without an interval [P7]. No consensus on interval treatment [P7].
- **Biomarkers unvalidated in HCC rechallenge:** PD-L1 expression, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, MSI, and mutational load influence *initial* ICI efficacy, but "little is known about their effects on ICI rechallenge in HCC patients" [P5]; predictive value of lymphatic/tertiary lymphoid structures in HCC rechallenge "remains unclear" [P8].
- **No head-to-head randomized comparison vs TKIs:** most data are retrospective/real-world; one retrospective study showed median post-progression survival of 14.9 vs 8.4 months (rechallenge vs TKI) but **not statistically significant (p = 0.25)** [P8]; the phase III CONTACT-03 trial in renal cell carcinoma found rechallenge not better than TKI monotherapy [P8]. Prospective randomized trials are "urgently needed" [P8].
- **Safety caveat:** irAE frequency may increase with rechallenge, though most events remain manageable with monitoring [P1][P2].
- **Mechanistic uncertainty:** rechallenge with anti-CTLA-4 alone after anti-PD-1/PD-L1 has not been reported, and simple switching "may not fully overcome" resistance mechanisms [P3].

**Not covered by the evidence:** no quantitative pooled benefit rate for "all-comers," and no data on several candidate biomarkers (ctDNA, HLA genotype, autoantibodies) specifically in HCC rechallenge — these are proposed as future directions only [P8].

# Why an Initial ICI Response Does Not Guarantee Continued Benefit in HCC

## Direct HCC evidence (partial)

The retrieved HCC-specific evidence addresses this question only indirectly, through the ICI **rechallenge** literature, and it does not provide a mechanistic account of secondary/acquired resistance in HCC.

- **Initial response is a prognostic factor, not a guarantee.** Lai et al. [29] (regimen 1) reported that a prior response to initial anti-PD-1 treatment was an independent protective factor for overall survival (O[S]) — but **not** for progression-free survival (PFS) — after ICI rechallenge in HCC [P2]. This dissociation implies that an initial response predicts longer survival without ensuring durable disease control.
- **Benefit after initial resistance is possible, so initial response is not a prerequisite either.** Some patients whose best overall response (BOR) to initial ICI was progressive disease (PD) still responded to rechallenge across regimens 1, 2, and 4 [P2]. Cho et al. [37] found all patients with initial PD also had PD at rechallenge (n = 3/3), whereas those with initial stable disease achieved a 60% disease control rate (n = 9/15) [P2].
- **Conflicting claim — Wong et al. [31] (regimen 2):** neither primary (PD as initial BOR) nor acquired resistance (SD/PR/CR as initial BOR) to initial ICI was associated with OS after rechallenge [P2]. *Limiting condition:* retrospective cohort, regimen 2; no further population/dose details stated in the passage.
- **Conflicting claim — Roessler et al. [33] (regimen 2):** a short duration of disease control on initial ICI did not necessarily preclude benefit from rechallenge [P2]. *Limiting condition:* not stated beyond regimen 2.
- **Safety-side caveat:** prior immune-related adverse events (irAEs; 7/32, 22%) recurred in 3 patients during dual-ICI rechallenge, mostly corticosteroid-manageable — prior irAEs are not an absolute contraindication but require individualized risk–benefit assessment [P2].
- **Rechallenge framing:** ICI rechallenge is described as a rational option for *selected* HCC patients after initial ICI resistance or discontinuation [S2], which presupposes that initial benefit can be lost.

**Not covered by the HCC evidence:** the biological mechanisms of acquired resistance in HCC, the frequency of secondary loss of response in HCC, and predictive biomarkers (PD-L1, tertiary lymphoid structures, lymphocyte infiltration, microsatellite stability, mutational load) — the review explicitly states that little is known about their effects on rechallenge in HCC, although they influence initial ICI effectiveness [P2].

## Mechanistic context from non-HCC evidence (transferable only by analogy)

- **Adaptive resistance as a general explanation for "response then progression":** compensatory IFN-γ signaling induces JAK–STAT-dependent PD-L1 upregulation, creating a negative feedback loop; this "provides a mechanistic explanation for the clinical pattern of an initial response followed by later disease progression in patients receiving anti-PD-1 therapy" [P3]. # EV Heterogeneity as a Barrier to Clinical Translation in Breast Cancer

## Core claim (breast cancer–specific evidence)

The breast cancer review states directly that "the full scope of EV function in BC metastasis remains unclear, and their inherent heterogeneity and molecular complexity present considerable barriers to clinical translation" [P6]. The same review attributes the gap between experimental findings and real-world outcomes partly to "the intrinsic heterogeneity of EV populations," alongside the difficulty of replicating cancer biology in functional studies [P7]. ## Mechanistic basis of the heterogeneity

EVs are classified into subpopulations by size and biology — sEVs/exosomes (~50–200 nm), lEVs (~150–500 nm), and apoptotic bodies (~500–4000 nm) — with overlapping size ranges; commonly used isolation methods also co-recover non-vesicular particles such as exomeres and supermeres, so sEV/lEV cannot be used interchangeably with exosome/microvesicle [P7]. Distinct subpopulations (sEVs, lEVs, apoptotic bodies) play distinct roles in tumour progression and metastasis [P7]. The proposed response is single-EV analysis (nano-flow cytometry, droplet-based assays, Raman spectrometry, aptamer-based detection, single-EV imaging) to resolve vesicle heterogeneity and identify metastasis-specific subpopulations "obscured in conventional bulk EV studies" [P7].

# Traditional Adenoma–Carcinoma Model vs. Contemporary CRC Research

## 1. The traditional model (foundational framework)

The classical adenoma–carcinoma sequence describes colorectal tumorigenesis as cumulative molecular alterations unfolding over time [P1]. In the conventional sporadic model, early APC loss and Wnt-pathway activation are followed by additional alterations—KRAS activation, 18q loss involving SMAD4/DCC, and TP53 inactivation—though the order is not invariant [P4]. Morphologically this corresponds to progression from normal mucosa through polypoid adenoma to invasive carcinoma, enabling colonoscopic detection and polypectomy [P4]. # Why Reproducibility Is a Central Challenge in AI Biomarker Discovery

## 1. It is identified as an unsolved, field-defining problem
Reproducibility is described as "one of the most significant unsolved challenges in AI-powered biomarker research" [P2], and more broadly as "a central challenge in biomarker development" [P1]. The core empirical pattern is that biomarkers performing well in discovery datasets "often show declines in accuracy, calibration, or clinical utility when evaluated across independent cohorts, health systems, or measurement platforms" [P2].

## 2. Sources of non-reproducibility in measured signals
Measured signals are "susceptible to cohort-specific effects, pre-analytical variability, platform drift, batch effects, and confounding factors related to concomitant diseases and treatment" [P1]. In multi-omics specifically, insufficient standardization of sample collection, preprocessing, quality control, and cross-platform normalization "limit[s] reproducibility across independent studies" [P4].

## 3. High dimensionality and overfitting
High-dimensional feature domains "increase the risk of overfitting when sample sizes are modest and analytical flexibility is high" [P1]; high dimensionality frequently exceeds available sample sizes, reducing generalizability [P4]. In discovery settings, "thousands of associated features may appear predictive, but only a subset will be stable under perturbation" [P7].

## 4. AI-specific failure modes: bias, confounding, and leakage
Richer datasets "create new opportunities for bias and error"; region-specific signatures, hidden confounding factors, and label leakage "can produce seemingly accurate models that fail when evaluated in independent cohorts or real-world settings" [P1]. Models may learn superficial correlations with strong development performance but no biological relevance or robustness [P1]. In microbiome work, a model may learn "batch, diet, medication, sequencing center, or geography rather than transferable biology" [P3].

## 5. Lack of transparency undermines reproducibility
AI-based biomarkers require explicit specification of cohort definition, endpoint labeling, preprocessing decisions, missing-data handling, model development choices, and evaluation protocols [P1]. "The fact that a lack of transparency weakens reproducibility has led to the development of AI-specific reporting frameworks and bias assessment tools" [P1].

## 6. What reproducibility must encompass (validation-phase requirement)
In the validation phase, "the key challenge is demonstrating robustness, transparency, and generalizability across diverse cohorts and real-world settings" [P1]. Reproducibility "should encompass stability across populations, consistency across technical platforms, and the preservation of clinical utility in independent settings" [P2]. Inter-site generalization is argued to matter more than intra-cohort performance [P7].

## 7. Why it matters translationally
Predictive performance alone is "increasingly seen as insufficient" [P2]; evaluation often relies on discrimination measures (e.g., AUC) without showing improved patient management or outcomes [P1]. Unstable feature sets "weaken biological interpretation and render subsequent validation inefficient" [P7]. Successful translation therefore depends on "rigorous validation, mechanistic interpretation, and demonstration of reproducible biological relevance" [P1].

## 8. Limits of current evidence infrastructure
Large collaborative consortia, benchmark datasets, and multicenter validation initiatives "often fail to fully reflect the diversity and complexity of real-world clinical settings" [P2]. Prospective validation in large, ethnically diverse cohorts remains limited, and many published biomarkers have not undergone external validation [P4].

# Nitric Oxide Synthesis by NOS Enzymes

## Core reaction and stoichiometry
NOS enzymes catalyze NO synthesis **from L-arginine and molecular oxygen in the presence of NADPH, with L-citrulline as a coproduct** [P1]. The reaction is a **two-step process**: L-arginine is first hydroxylated to N-hydroxy-L-arginine, which is then oxidized to yield NO and L-citrulline [P1]. This is also stated for the endothelial isoform specifically: NO is synthesized from L-arginine in vascular endothelial cells under the catalysis of eNOS [P7].

## Structural requirements
- Active NOS is a **homodimer**, each monomer comprising a reductase domain and an oxygenase domain [P1].
- NOS contains covalently bound **heme** plus the flavin cofactors **FAD and FMN** [P1].
- Activity requires **tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4)**, positioned between the two domains of a monomer but contacting the opposing monomer, contributing to dimer stabilization [P1].
- Dimer formation is stabilized by a **Zn²⁺ ion** coordinated by four cysteines, two from each monomer [P1].
- All NOS isoenzymes are synthesized as monomers; dimerization requires heme, L-arginine, and BH4, with BH4 exerting a stronger stabilizing effect than L-arginine [P3].

## Inter-monomer electron transfer
NO synthesis requires **cooperation between both monomers**: electrons from NADPH pass through FAD and FMN in the reductase domain of one monomer to the heme iron in the oxygenase domain of the *other* monomer [P1]. Several mechanistic aspects remain incompletely understood [P1].

## Isoform-specific control of output
- NOS1 and NOS3 require relatively high Ca²⁺ (~400 nM); at physiological cytoplasmic Ca²⁺ (~100 nM) their NO production is low — "calcium-dependent, low-output" isoenzymes [P1].
- NOS2 binds calmodulin tightly and requires ~tenfold lower Ca²⁺, so Ca²⁺ is generally not limiting; NOS2 produces large amounts of NO continuously for hours, ceasing only upon enzyme degradation — "calcium-independent, high-output" [P1].

## Regulation of the synthetic machinery (assembly and catalytic activity)
Because NO is broadly bioactive and potentially cytotoxic, especially from high-output NOS2, its production must be tightly regulated [P2]. NOS2 is controlled predominantly at transcriptional and post-transcriptional levels rather than by modulating enzymatic activity [P2]. At the protein level, NOS2 activity is controlled through **dimer assembly, subcellular localization, catalytic activity, and protein turnover**, modulated by protein–protein interactions and post-translational modifications (tyrosine nitration, S-nitrosylation, phosphorylation, ubiquitination, acylation) [P5]. NOS2 forms the least stable dimers and is most prone to disassembly; excessive NO can inhibit NOS2 dimerization by limiting heme availability, and NO-derived species can interfere with dimer formation via coordination with heme Fe³⁺ [P3]. Heme incorporation is ATP-dependent and facilitated by HSP90A [P3].

## Uncoupling: when the reaction fails to produce NO
When the substrate L-arginine or the cofactor BH4 is limited, **eNOS uncouples and reduces molecular oxygen to superoxide instead of producing NO** [P6]. Uncoupling is rarely complete, so the same enzyme can generate NO and superoxide simultaneously, which combine at a near diffusion-limited rate to form peroxynitrite [P6]. Folate can prevent eNOS uncoupling and protect against eNOS dysfunction [P7].

## Context-dependent consequences of the synthesized NO
The biological effects of NOS-derived NO depend on concentration, enzymatic/cellular source, and local microenvironment [P2]. The traditional constitutive (low-output, physiological) versus inducible (high-output, pro-inflammatory) dichotomy is increasingly viewed as insufficient, as NOS2 activation outcomes are highly context dependent [P2]. Regulation of NOS2 extends well beyond the classical IFNγ/STAT1 and NF-κB pathways, involving epigenetic mechanisms, microRNAs, lncRNAs, mRNA stability, protein turnover, and trafficking, as well as tissue-specific factors (microbial metabolites, hypoxia, iron availability, ER stress, neuroimmune signaling, immunometabolic reprogramming) [P4]. NOS2 expression is also markedly heterogeneous across epithelial, stromal, endothelial, and immune-cell populations, with non-equivalent functions by cell type [P4].

## Local/physiological example of NOS1-derived NO synthesis
In the kidney, luminal glucose uptake through macula densa SGLT1 transporters directly upregulates NOS1; the resulting NO signal promotes vasodilation and suppresses tubuloglomerular feedback [P8].

# Conditions for Calling an AI Biomarker Clinically Useful

## 1. Evidence-hierarchy progression (discovery → external → prospective → clinical utility → regulatory adoption)

A biomarker must advance through staged validation before it can be termed clinically useful. Discovery-level signals from single or aggregated retrospective cohorts are "highly vulnerable to overfitting, aggregate effect, and cohort-specific confounding" and reflect "intrinsic separability rather than generalizable disease biology" [P7]. External validation in independent cohorts is required, though it "does not guarantee clinical significance if the patient spectrum, treatment models, or outcome definitions differ from the intended use cases" [P7]. Prospective validation must demonstrate operational feasibility and workflow integration, but "prospective accuracy does not automatically imply clinical benefit" [P7]. Clinical utility requires evidence that biomarker-guided decisions improve patient outcomes or resource allocation versus standard care, assessed via decision curve analysis, net utility, pragmatic trials, or embedded application studies [P7]. Finally, regulatory adoption requires sustained real-world performance, workflow integration, and post-market oversight—with lifecycle oversight rather than one-off validation for adaptive systems [P7]. Table 4 maps each evidence level to study design, dataset type, what is demonstrated, common pitfalls, and suitable publication claims [P7].

## 2. Analytical validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility (Table 11)

Table 11 specifies three validation domains with assigned responsibility and typical evidence: analytical validity (analysis + preprocessing; laboratory + vendor; accuracy, reproducibility; failure point = batch effects), clinical validity (biomarker–outcome correlation; developers; external cohorts; failure point = spectrum bias), and clinical utility (decision benefit; trial sponsors; interventional trials; failure point = no impact on workflow) [P6]. It further requires algorithm governance (model stability; manufacturers; version control audits; failure point = drift post-distribution) and post-marketing surveillance (safety and bias; institutions; real-world monitoring; failure point = recalibration neglected) [P6]. Meeting these is "vital not only for regulatory approval but also for sustainable clinical reliability" [P6].

## 3. Biological/mechanistic grounding

Correlational biomarkers, while clinically useful, "are fragile when used to guide treatment, predict response mechanisms, or serve as surrogate endpoints"; mechanistic discovery requires constraints linking features to biological processes, integrating computational evidence with biological plausibility, perturbation consistency, and pathway coherence [P3]. Feature attribution without such integration "risks generating compelling narratives not supported by causal biology" [P3]. Biomarkers reflecting causal disease processes are more likely to generalize and remain stable under intervention than those from correlational signatures alone [P8].

## 4. Multimodal integration driven by biological hypotheses

Multimodal integration offers advantages when pathology spans molecular-to-organ scales, but "integration should be driven by biological hypotheses and empirical probability, rather than the indiscriminate aggregation of heterogeneous features" [P8]. In neurodegeneration, multimodal fusion improves prediction of MCI-to-dementia transition and disease subtyping, but generalization is "sensitive to scanner protocols, cohort composition, and real-world variability" [P5].

## 5. Workflow integration and interpretability thresholds

"Even analytically validated biomarkers can fail clinically if they cannot be integrated into routine workflows" [P9]. Requirements include compatibility with laboratory information systems, imaging platforms, and electronic health records, plus clearly defined clinical action thresholds; translating continuous risk scores into actionable categories is "one of the biggest barriers to adoption" [P9]. Interpretability requirements are context-dependent: mechanistic transparency may not be needed for low-risk screening, while therapeutic decision support often requires description of contributing features or biological pathways; over-reliance on post-hoc annotations lacking biological basis "can create false reassurance instead of true understanding" [P9].

## 6. Real-world evidence and post-implementation monitoring

After transition to practice, AI biomarkers must be evaluated under real-world conditions of heterogeneous populations, evolving practice, and variable data quality; RWE can assess whether biomarker-guided decisions improve outcomes, reduce costs, or change treatment models versus standard care [P1]. Monitoring must cover clinical impact, adverse events, and equity across subpopulations, since model drift, test changes, and epidemiological shifts can degrade performance and may require recalibration or retraining under regulatory oversight [P1]. RWE can also refine thresholds, decision rules, and patient selection by revealing discrepancies between trial performance and real-world efficacy [P1].

## 7. Demonstrated clinical benefit, not assumed utility

Success "should be defined not only by prediction accuracy but also by demonstrable clinical benefit," using decision analysis metrics, workflow integration, and patient-relevant outcomes [P8]. Common pitfalls include assuming statistical association has therapeutic significance, relying solely on internal cross-validation, and neglecting population diversity and health-system variability [P8]. A parallel formulation from the mitochondrial-biomarker literature states that "clinical utility must be demonstrated rather than assumed"—a useful test must classify a reproducible biological phenotype, predict prognosis or treatment response, and improve outcomes when used to guide care; until then, such biomarkers "should remain research tools" [P10].

## 8. Methodological preconditions (from the causal-inference/SEM evidence)

Although derived from Mendelian randomization and SEM rather than AI biomarkers directly, two passages specify formal preconditions for valid inference that parallel the "biological grounding" requirement. MR requires three conditions—relevance, exchangeability, and exclusion restriction—and violation of exclusion restriction (e.g., pleiotropic pathways) biases causal estimates [P2]. SEM requires that all specified relationships be theoretically justified, that measurement models demonstrate reliability and validity, and that structural relationships be appropriately modeled (generally linear unless specified otherwise) [P4]. These are cited as methodological analogues; the evidence does not state that they are formal requirements for AI biomarker approval.

## 9. Accountability and governance

AI biomarkers distribute responsibility among developers, data providers, and institutions; regulatory and legal frameworks increasingly require documentation of intended use, decision-support limitations, and clinician override mechanisms, with clinicians retaining ultimate responsibility and institutions ensuring comparable standards of evidence and safety to other diagnostic technologies [P6].

# ICI Rechallenge Strategies and the Observed ORR Difference (HCC)

## 1. The four strategies and their ORRs

Four combination strategies are defined by the drug selection in initial versus rechallenge treatment [P1]:

| Strategy | Initial ICI | Rechallenge regimen | n (%) | ORR | DCR | mPFS |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | anti-PD-1 | targeted therapy + anti-PD-L1 | 138 (36.0%) | 17.4% | 64.5% | 5.2–5.6 mo |
| 2 | targeted + anti-PD-L1 | ipilimumab + nivolumab | 100 (26.1%) | 18.0% | 45.0% | 2.4–3.0 mo |
| 3 | bevacizumab + atezolizumab | tremelimumab + durvalumab | 132 (34.5%) | 6.8% | 40.2% | 2.0–4.0 mo |
| 4 | bevacizumab + atezolizumab | same regimen (atezolizumab + bevacizumab) | 13 (3.4%) | 15.0% | 54.0% | 4.7 mo |

All values from [P1]; the review also states that strategies 1 and 2 achieved relatively higher ORR and more favorable outcomes than strategies 3 and 4, and that regimen 1 and 2 appeared to offer a better efficacy–safety balance [P1]. The four-strategy taxonomy itself is summarized in the abstract [P2].

## 2. Interpretation of the ORR difference

- **Direction of the difference:** The spread in ORR (6.8%–18.0%) tracks the strategy used, with the anti-PD-1→targeted/anti-PD-L1 switch (strategy 1) and the ipilimumab–nivolumab dual-ICI switch (strategy 2) at the upper end, and the CTLA-4/PD-L1 combination after bevacizumab–atezolizumab (strategy 3) at the lower end [P1].
- **Caveat on statistical inference:** The review explicitly states that no statistical comparisons were performed across regimens, that the evidence is mainly retrospective with substantial heterogeneity, and that findings should be interpreted with caution [P1]. The ORR difference is therefore descriptive, not a tested between-regimen effect.
- **Pooled context:** Across all rechallenge studies the ORR was 13.8%, lower than the 20.3% ORR of initial ICI treatment, attributed to higher tumor burden and poorer performance status at rechallenge [P6]. Individual studies nonetheless reported higher ORR on rechallenge than on initial therapy (e.g., 26% vs 22%; 22% vs 6%) [P6], indicating that the strategy-level ORR differences sit within a heterogeneous pooled picture.

## 3. Factors beyond strategy that could confound the ORR comparison

- **Rechallenge interval:** Intervals >1 month were associated with ORR 19.1%, DCR 62.5%, and mPFS 3.7–5.4 months, versus ORR 20.0%, DCR 40.0%, and mPFS 2.9–3.0 months for intervals <1 month [P7]. Because interval length varied across the studies underpinning the four strategies, timing—not only drug selection—may contribute to the observed ORR/DCR differences [P7]. No study reported direct rechallenge without an interval [P7].
- **Patient selection:** Benefit appears more frequent in patients with preserved liver function, age <60 years, and lower tumor burden, though this requires cautious interpretation due to interstudy heterogeneity and selection bias [P2].
- **Decision-making context:** Rechallenge decisions depend on multiple patient-, tumor-, and treatment-specific factors with no validated risk-stratification tool [P4]; the evidence base is retrospective with selection bias and confounding by indication [P4]. This limits attribution of ORR differences to the regimen alone.
- **Comparator uncertainty:** No head-to-head study compares ICI rechallenge with TKIs in HCC; an international retrospective study reported median post-progression survival of 14.9 vs 8.4 months (p = 0.25), and the phase III CONTACT-03 trial in renal cell carcinoma found rechallenge not superior to TKI monotherapy [P3]. Thus the ORR advantage of strategies 1–2 has not been benchmarked against non-ICI salvage.

## 4. Safety dimension accompanying the ORR difference

Grade ≥3 irAE rates were 18.8% (strategy 1), 16.4% (strategy 2), 24.3% (strategy 3), and 15.0% (strategy 4), all within 15.0%–24.3% [P1]. The review concludes that combination strategies, particularly regimens 1 and 2, offer a more favorable efficacy–safety balance [P1], and that rechallenge is a rational option for selected patients with manageable irAEs under vigilant monitoring [P5]. General rechallenge literature likewise notes that recurrence risk (30–50%) and predictors of recurrence are poorly defined and that prophylactic immunosuppression and observation duration remain unresolved [P4]; for pneumonitis specifically, rechallenge is recommended only after complete resolution of grade 2 ICI-P, and mitigation strategies remain unstudied [P8].

## 5. Not covered by the evidence

- No statistical test, confidence intervals, or multivariable adjustment for the between-strategy ORR differences is reported [P1].
- No data link the four strategies to biomarker-defined subgroups (e.g., ctDNA, tertiary lymphoid structures), as these remain exploratory in rechallenge [P3].
- The retrieved evidence contains no figure/table-level ORR data beyond those cited from the text (Fig. 2c–e is referenced but its values are only reported in the prose) [P1].
- One retrieved passage concerns microbiome-directed strategies in colorectal cancer and is not relevant to ICI rechallenge ORR [P9]; it is noted here only to confirm it was reviewed and excluded as non-supporting.

# EV Subpopulations in Breast Cancer Metastasis and Diagnosis

## 1. Subpopulation classification and general roles

In BC, distinct EV subpopulations — mainly small EVs (sEVs), large EVs (lEVs), and apoptotic bodies — play distinct roles in promoting tumour progression and metastasis [P1]. Size-based categories are used per MISEV guidelines: sEVs/exosomes ~50–200 nm, lEVs ~150–500 nm, apoptotic bodies ~500–4000 nm; the authors caution that size ranges overlap and isolation methods may co-recover non-vesicular particles (exomeres, supermeres) [P1]. Both sEVs and lEVs deliver bioactive cargo linked to progression, metastasis, and angiogenesis [P1]. Figure 1 depicts BC cells releasing sEVs and lEVs that remodel the TME via immune suppression, migration and invasion, promoting pre-metastatic niche (PMN) formation and organotropic niche conditioning [P4].

## 2. sEV contributions to metastasis

- **PMN and immune reprogramming:** BC-derived sEV ncRNAs reprogram macrophages toward tumour-associated phenotypes (e.g., miR-33, miR-130, circ-0100519 → TAM activation; miR-138-5p → KDM6B suppression and TNBC lung metastasis; RAB5A-enhanced miR-21 transfer → PELI1 suppression) [P2]. sEV miR-27a-3p suppresses MAGI2/PTEN, increasing PD-L1 and T-cell apoptosis (immune evasion) [P2].
- **Stromal crosstalk:** TNBC sEV miR-125b and miR-370-3p drive fibroblast differentiation into CAFs; CAF-derived sEV miR-500a-5p/miR-18b enhance metastatic features bidirectionally [P2].
- **Vascular/PMN:** sEV miR-105 inhibits ZO-1, disrupting the endothelial barrier [P2].
- **Invasion and organotropism:** miR-10b, miR-222, NEAT1, MALAT1, miR-7641, miR-361-3p promote invasion/migration [P2]; organ-specific examples include miR-200 (lung), miR-4443 (liver), miR-1246/miR-1290/miR-301a-3p (brain), and miR-940/miR-19a/IBSP (bone) [P2].
- **Caveat:** RNA cargoes are considered plausible vesicular mediators, but vesicular delivery is "in most cases, not formally demonstrated" [P2].
- **Protein cargo (Table 2):** e.g., integrins (PMN/organotropism), CEMIP (brain/vascular niche), TSP1, Survivin, EPHA2, PD-L1 (sEV/lEV) [P7].

## 3. lEV contributions to metastasis

PD-L1-positive lEVs from TNBC patients suppress cytotoxic T cells and drive M2-like polarisation via TBK1/STAT6; irradiation-induced PD-L1 lEVs act partly PD-L1-dependently [P7]. lEV CD44 reduces focal adhesions and induces actin rearrangement in low-metastatic cells [P7]. Tg2-enriched lEVs activate fibroblasts and increase tumour stiffness [P7]. Chemotherapy increases phosphatidylserine-exposing lEVs that promote platelet activation, endothelial permeability, and transendothelial migration [P7]. Comparative proteomics show overlapping but partly lEV-enriched proteins, with profiles varying by subpopulation and cell line [P7]. sEVs appear more associated with organotropism and PMN conditioning, whereas lEV involvement is more evident under therapy-induced stress [P7]. Migrasomes cannot yet be reliably separated from lEVs, so their metastasis attribution is uncertain [P7].

## 4. Diagnostic and biomarker potential

Growing evidence supports EVs as diagnostic/prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets, though heterogeneity and molecular complexity impede clinical translation [P5]. Table 3 contrasts biomarker potential: sEVs have multiple circulating RNAs/proteins evaluated in clinical samples, whereas lEVs show emerging but limited clinical evidence [P7]. Subtype-specific lipid profiles may provide additional biomarkers for BC detection and classification, though distribution across subpopulations remains unresolved [P7]. Single-EV analysis (nano-flow cytometry, droplet assays, Raman spectrometry, aptamer detection, single-EV imaging) is proposed to resolve heterogeneity and identify metastasis-specific subpopulations obscured in bulk studies [P1]. Clinical translation remains poor (Phase I oncology success ~3.4%) [P1].
